readerTitle: Why a new dish now takes eleven weeks
caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑 그룹, 소프트웨어 회사) + 실제 기업 자료 (Amazon 2015 주주서한, Ritz-Carlton 직원 재량권)
insight: 회사가 느려지는 이유는 규모가 아니라 되돌릴 수 있는 결정까지 되돌릴 수 없는 결정처럼 무겁게 다루기 때문이다. 결정의 무게를 되돌리기 쉬운 정도에 맞추면 커져도 빠르다.
misconception: 회사가 커지면 느려지는 건 어쩔 수 없다. 모든 결정에 승인 단계를 늘리면 실수가 줄어 더 안전하다.

sources.text: Jeff Bezos, 2015 Letter to Amazon Shareholders (Type 1 / Type 2 decisions, one-way and two-way doors)
Ritz-Carlton 직원 재량권 정책 (고객 1인당 최대 $2,000) 관련 회사 자료 및 언론 보도
레스토랑 그룹과 소프트웨어 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Bezos 2015 주주서한의 Type 1(되돌릴 수 없는, one-way door)과 Type 2(되돌릴 수 있는, two-way door) 구분, 그리고 조직이 커지면 Type 2 결정에도 무거운 절차를 쓰는 경향이 생겨 느려지고 실험을 피하게 된다는 내용을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 직접 인용 없이 요약만 썼습니다.
Ritz-Carlton의 '직원이 상사 승인 없이 고객 1인당 최대 $2,000까지 쓸 수 있다'는 정책은 여러 경영 사례와 언론에 널리 소개되었지만, 현재도 유지되는지는 확인이 필요합니다. 카드에는 'has long been reported'로 적었습니다.
레스토랑의 '11주', 매장 6곳, 소프트웨어 회사의 80명·4개 팀 승인 등은 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Why a new dish now takes eleven weeks
body: In year one, the chef tried a new dish on a Tuesday. If guests loved it, it stayed. If not, it was gone by Friday.
Six restaurants later, a new dish needs a tasting panel, a costing review, a photo shoot and the founder's sign-off. It takes eleven weeks. Nobody added a bad rule. So where did the speed go?

image.label: A chef waiting while a dish passes through a long line of approvers
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 셰프가 접시 하나를 들고 서 있고, 그 앞에 도장을 든 사람 네 명이 줄지어 서 있음. 벽 달력에 11주가 표시됨. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: A manager wants to test a lunch special.
body: You own the six-restaurant group. One location manager wants to try a cheaper weekday lunch set to fill empty tables.
How should this kind of request be handled from now on?

options.text: Send it through the central tasting panel, like every menu change
options.feedback: Consistent and safe, but a two-week test now waits months. Managers stop suggesting ideas when every one takes a quarter.

options.text: Let managers run short tests at one location within set cost and safety limits. The panel reviews only permanent, group-wide changes.
options.feedback: You keep the careful review for changes that are hard to undo and give speed to the ones that aren't. The cost: some tests will flop in public.

options.text: Have managers text you directly for a quick yes or no
options.feedback: Fast today, while you have time to answer. With more locations, you become the queue everyone waits in.

cards.title: Every decision got the same heavy treatment.
body: Each step was added for a good reason. The tasting panel came after a dish failed at three locations. The costing review came after a margin scare.
But the rules didn't ask *what kind* of decision it was. A one-week special and a permanent change to all six menus went through the same eleven-week path.
The group didn't slow down because it grew. It slowed down because **small, undoable choices** started carrying the weight of big ones.

cards.title: Match the weight of a decision to how easily it can be undone.
body: Jeff Bezos described this in Amazon's 2015 letter to shareholders. Some decisions are **one-way doors**: hard or impossible to reverse. They deserve slow, careful thought. Most are two-way doors: if you're wrong, you walk back through.
His warning was that growing companies tend to use the slow process for both kinds. The result is slowness, too little experimenting and fear of trying things.

image.label: Two doors: a heavy one-way door and a light swinging door
image.brief: 두 개의 문 인포그래픽. 왼쪽은 무거운 금고형 문에 "One-way: slow, careful", 오른쪽은 양쪽으로 열리는 가벼운 스윙 문에 "Two-way: fast, close to the work". 로고 없음.

cards.title: Three questions sort the decision.
body: Before choosing how much process a decision gets, ask:
list: **Can we undo it?** A one-week special, yes. A ten-year lease, no.
**What does being wrong cost?** A few unsold plates, or your reputation?
**Who knows the most?** Often the person closest to the customer, not the person at the top.
cards.callout: Undoable, cheap to get wrong, best known locally: decide fast, close to the work.

cards.title: Pushing small decisions down, on purpose.
body: Ritz-Carlton has long been reported to let staff spend up to $2,000 per guest to fix a problem without asking a manager. A cold room or a missed booking gets fixed in minutes, not after a chain of approvals.
The hotel isn't careless with money. It decided in advance which choices are two-way doors and set a clear limit around them.
cards.softwareNote: Software teams do this with *feature flags*: a switch that turns a new feature on for a few users and off again in seconds. It turns many risky launches into two-way doors.

cards.title: Not every door swings back.
body: Some choices only look reversible. A price cut is easy to announce and hard to take back, because customers remember. A new hire can be let go, but the cost to the team is real.
And some doors are truly one-way: food safety, major contracts, leaders you hire. Moving fast there is not speed. It's risk.
Speed also needs limits people can see. Without clear boundaries, staff either freeze or guess.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your 80-person company sells scheduling software. Changing the text on one onboarding screen needs sign-off from product, design, marketing and legal. A team wants to test a shorter sign-up flow with 10% of new users.

options.text: Let the team run the test behind a feature flag, with legal review only for changes to terms or data collection
options.feedback: The test can be switched off in seconds, so it gets a light path. The parts that are hard to undo still get the careful review.

options.text: Keep all four sign-offs. The onboarding flow is too important to risk
options.feedback: It protects the screen, but every small test now costs weeks. Your rivals learn ten times while you learn once.

options.text: Remove all sign-offs for anything product touches
options.feedback: Very fast, but it also removes review from one-way doors, like what data you collect. Sort decisions instead of dropping every check.

cards.title: Go slow on one-way doors. Go fast on everything else.
body: Growing companies stay fast when they stop treating every choice like a big one.
**Try it today:** list the last five decisions that waited for your approval. Mark each one: could it be undone within a week? For each yes, name who could decide it without you.
